EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
In February 2014, NewGen Strategies & Solutions, LLC  (“NewGen”) was retained by the City 
of Murphy (“City”) to perform a Water and Sewer Rate Study (“Study”).  As part of this Study, 
NewGen’s Project Team (“Project Team”) was requested to forecast revenue requirements 
and rates from Fiscal Year (“FY”) 2014 through FY 2019.   
As part of the Study, the Project Team considered the following policy directives  as outlined 
by the City Council: 
 The Utilities Fund currently makes a transfer to the General Fund each year for expenses 
related to shared staffing or other costs incurred by the Utility but paid by the General 
Fund.  The City would like to consider decreasing the transfer by 50%.   
 The City receives its water supply and wastewater treatment from the North Texas 
Municipal Water District (“NTMWD”).  The cost of the water and wastewater is currently 
embedded in the customer rates.  The City would like to co nsider itemizing the NTMWD 
charge as a separate rate component to increase transparency in rate design.   
 The City desires to decrease the minimum charge to both water and wastewater 
customers, assuming such action is not financially detrimental to the utility.  
 The City would like to establish sewer charges based on an assumption of domestic 
strength and quality.   
 A debt service coverage ratio (“DSCR”) of at least 1.10 must be maintained. 
 The Utility must maintain a Fund Balance requirement of 25% of total expenditures. 
The Project Team  calculated a five -year revenue requirement  using the FY 2014 budget as 
the test year.  As a result of the analysis performed for the City, the Proj ect Team concluded, 
assuming normal precipitation conditions, that on a comb ined basis the City’s current rate 
revenues are insufficient to fund the cost of service.  In addition, the revenue generated 
through rates does not produce adequate revenue to meet the Fund Balance r equirement 
policy.  
Based on the analysis conducted  and in consideration of the City Council’s policy directives, 
the Project Team concluded the following: 
 The Project Team has determined that decreasing the General Fund transfer  could have a 
significant impact on the General Fund’s available resources and may n ot be in the best 
financial interest of the utility’s average customer. 
 As a result of itemizing the NTMWD cost, i t has been determined that sewer customer 
rates are currently not reflecting the cost of treatment. 
 Under the current rate structure, a signif icant portion of the water and wastewater 
revenue is recovered in the base charge for the City port ion of the rates , and some 
minimal adjustment to the fixed portion of the rate structure can be considered .  
However, it is noted by the Project Team that a reduction in the base charge will create 
instability in the revenue stream as more revenue will need to be generated in the 
volumetric rates.  Relying on revenues based on customer usage is less reliable due to the 
unpredictability of rainfall and water usage. 
 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
 
2 City of Murphy Final Report 
 The Capital Improvement Plan (“CIP”) provided by the City includes $9.2 million in 
estimated future costs.  The City will need to ensure there are sufficient funds available to 
fund the Capital Investments. 
 Establishing sewer charges based on an assumption of domestic strength and quality 
would require the rate to be the same for all customer classes. 
 The current meter charges do not reflect the American Water Works Association’s 
(“AWWA”) recommended flow capacitie s.  It is the recommendation of the Project Team 
that the rates be adjusted to reflect AWWA’s standard practice in setting meter charges. 
 The adopted rate structure does not include a standardized percentage differential 
between volumetric rate blocks.  Th e Project Team is recommending a standard 15% 
increase between blocks. 
The current rates are made up of two components:  the City portion and the NTWMD 
portion.  The NTWMD rate is a pass -through cost which the City cannot change.  Therefore , 
the Project Te am isolated the NTMWD’s portion of the rates in order to calculate the City’s 
portion of the  rates.  It is the Project Team’s recommendation that the  City portion of the  
rates be adjusted to meet the requirements of the City Council as well as ensure suffi cient 
revenue is available to meet fiscal needs.   In order the achieve these objectives, t he City 
needs to generate additional revenue of approximately $757,716, or 14.7%, in FY 2015. 
The Project Team has reviewed the projected revenue requirement and recommends making 
the following adjustments to the rates: 
 Water:   
 For all customer classes, decrease the minimum bill by $5.00, from $25.00 to $20.00 
for ¾” meters.  Use the AWWA meter equivalencies based on a ¾” meter to increase 
the rates for all other meter sizes.   
 For Residential customers, increase the first rate block from $2.95 to $3.80.  Design 
the rates with a 15% rate increase between the blocks. 
 For Residential Sprinkler customers, increase the first rate block from $3.95 to $4.13.  
As with Residential customers, increase the rate 15% for each rate block. 
 Maintain the current volumetric rate blocks.   
 Wastewater: 
 For all customer classes, decrease the minimum bill to $18.00 from $20.00. 
 Adopt a standard volumetric rate of $3.02 for all customer classes.

Section 1 
INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND 
Introduction 
In February 2014, New Gen Strategies & Solutions, LLC  (“NewGen”) was retained by the City 
of Murphy (“City”) to perform a Water and Sewer Rate Study (“Study”).  As part of this Study, 
NewGen’s Project Team (“Project Team”) was requested to forecast revenue requirements 
and rates from Fiscal Year (“FY”) 2014 through FY 2019.  This final report describes the 
analysis performed for the City and makes rec ommendations with respect to rates to be 
charged to the City’s water and sewer customers.  This report consists of four sections and 
an Executive Summary.  Also attached are four (4) appendices which supplement the findings 
of this report. 
Following the Executive Summary, Section I provides the introduction and background for 
the Study.  Section II discusses the development of the revenue requirement(s) through FY 
2019.  Section III discusses the estimated rates needed to recover the estimated revenue 
requirement(s).  Finally, Section IV offers recommendations based on the Study’s findings. 
Regular reviews of the performance of a utility’s water and sewer rates are an integral part 
of the management of any water and sewer utility, and failure to monitor th e City’s rates can 
result in the need for significant rate actions.  Our Project Team recommends that, going 
forward, the City regularly monitor and review the performance of its adopted rates and 
perform rate adjustments in a timely manner so as to preser ve the financial integrity of the 
water and sewer utility. 
The analysis performed by NewGen is designed to take into account the foreseeable changes 
from the current fiscal year (FY 2014) through FY 2019.  The goal is to construct a planning 
tool with whic h the City can gain an understanding of the issues that need to be addressed 
during the Study’s planning horizon.  A critical benefit is the quantification of the long -range 
impact of decisions being made today.  As with any forecast, assumptions must be m ade and 
the City should be aware that the actual rates required may be different from the projected 
rates outlined in this report due to unforeseen changes such as system growth, inflation, etc.  
In addition, it should be noted that this analysis is based on data provided by the City.  While 
this data has been reviewed and tested for accuracy to the extent possible, if the data relied 
on by the Project Team to produce this analysis is inaccurate and not reflective of the actual 
operation and/or financial condition of the City’s water and sewer system, then the results of 
this analysis may merit revision.  
Background 
A water and sewer utility is essentially a business run by a City and; therefore, should 
operate in a fiscally sound and prudent manner.  Servin g as the “Board of Directors” of the 
business, the City Council must currently contend with several issues which are impacting the 
financial integrity and stability of the City’s water and sewer utility.   
 
Section 1 
 
1-2 City of Murphy Final Report 
First, the City currently takes wholesale treated water from the North Texas Municipal Water 
District (“NTMWD”) and sends its collected sewer back to the NTMWD for treatment.  Under 
the City’s contracts with NTWMD, the supplier has the opportunity to annually adjust the 
rates charged to the City to ensure  they can cover the cost of providing service.  Failure to 
annually pass along these rate adjustments to the City’s retail customers can significantly 
impact the financial stability of the utility as more of its available resources are being 
devoted to the payment of wholesale costs.   
Second, based on conversations with City staff, as a result of not fully passing along cost 
increases from the wholesale supplier, the City’s available budget for general operations and 
maintenance expenses and capital improv ements has decreased over time.  Based on 
information from the City’s Capital Improvement Plan (“CIP”), the City is currently in need of 
approximately $8.2 million in water capital improvements and just under $1 million  in sewer 
capital improvements over the Study time period (adjusted for inflation).  Given the financial 
needs of the utility, an increase in rates is necessary to ensure the City has sufficient financial 
resources to cover the cost of providing service and fund needed capital improvements.  A 
listing of this CIP for the next five (5) year period is included in the attached Appendix A. 
Third, the City annually transfers funds from the General Fund to the Utility Fund to reflect 
payment for actual water use.  Based on the cost of service, the G eneral Fund’s annual use of 
water is estimated at approximately $190,000.  The City Council would like to consider a 50% 
reduction of the current funding level.  Assuming no reduction in General Fund expenditures, 
the reduction in transfer will need to be funded with another revenue source such as ad 
valorem or sales tax.   
Fourth, the City would like to consider reducing the customers’ minimum bill charges.  While 
doing so potentially relieves some of the financial burden on the City’s lower / fixed income  
customers, it exposes the City to a greater possibility of under -recovery of revenues.  A 
reduction in the base charge will create instability in the revenue stream as more revenue 
will need to be generated in the volumetric rates.  Relying on revenues ba sed on customer 
usage is less dependable due to the unpredictability of rainfall and water usage.  
Finally, based on the analysis conducted, and assuming normal precipitation conditions, the 
Project Team estimates that on a combined basis, the City’s current rates revenues are 
insufficient to fund the cost of service.  Furthermore, in the opinion of the  Project Team, the 
rate structure does not currently meet American Water Works Association (“ AWWA”) 
recommended flow capacities  within the base charge .  At this time, the Project Team 
recommends that the City amend the current rate structure and implement rate increases 
necessary to meet recommended standards and to produce additional rate revenues 
effective October of 2014.

Section 2 
REVENUE REQUIREMENT 
There are two primary ratemaking methodologies employed in the utility industry, the cash 
basis and the utility basis.  The primary difference between the cash basis and the utility 
basis involves the treatment of depreciation, return on invested capital, and debt service.  
The cash basis, which is the most common method used by municipalities, includes debt 
service but excludes depreciation and return on invested capital in the revenue requirement 
determination.  The cash basis focuses on meeting the cash demands of the utility.  The 
utility basis, most commonly used by private utilities, includes depreciation and return on 
invested capital, but excludes debt service from the revenue requirement determination.  
The cash basis is usually more easily understo od by municipalities since it follows the 
traditional cash-oriented budgeting practices used by governmental entities.  In addition, the 
cash basis is generally easier to explain to customers since the cash basis attempts to match 
revenue to expenditures.  In performing this analysis, the Project Team has utilized the cash 
basis to develop the City’s water and sewer revenue requirements. 
Test Year Revenue Requirement 
To develop the Rate Year Revenue Requirement (i.e., the first year for which rates are 
developed), NewGen utilized the adopted FY 2014 budget for the City.  To ensure the City’s 
budget accurately reflects the cost of providing water and sewer service, several adjustments 
were made to the budgeted numbers.  These are discussed in detail below: 
Cost of Water 
In order to separate the City rate from NTMWD pass -through rate, the Project Team must 
isolate NTWMD costs.  As a result, the budget was reduced by $1.88 million to account for 
the cost of water from the NTMWD.  This cost is recovered through  a separate pass-through 
rate which is determined by cost estimates from the NTMWD.  The remaining $793,058 is the 
value of the lost and unaccounted for water which is recovered through the City portion of 
the rates. 
Cost of Sewer Operation 
Similar to water, the sewer cost of treatment in the amount of $567,232 paid to the NTMWD 
was removed from the budget.  This expense will be recovered through the NTMWD pass -
through rate.  The remaining $168,268 reflects the cost of inflow and infiltration (“ I & I”). 
Debt Service 
The budgeted debt service included Principal and Interest (“P&I”) on the Murphy 
Wastewater Treatment Plant, Muddy Creek Interceptor, and Muddy Creek Wastewater 
Treatment Plant.  These costs are included in the NTMWD pass -through rate and, therefore, 
have been removed from the budget.  As a result, there is a net decrease in the budgeted 
value in the amount of $178,034. 
 
Section 2 
 
2-2 City of Murphy Final Report 
Cash Capital Outlays 
The City’s CIP estimates approximately $2.25 million in water and sewer capital 
improvements are needed in FY 2014.  The City plans to fund $4 17,576 using cash generated 
through rates , with the remainder of capital needs funded through future debt issuance .  
Therefore, this amount was added to the budget as an additional line item to develop the 
cost of service. 
Forecasted Revenue Requirement 
In determining the forecasted revenue requirements of the utility, the Project Team utilized 
the City’s adopted FY 2014 budget, adjusted as discussed above, as the basis for the revenue 
requirement projections through FY 2019.  Discussions were held with City staff to determine 
the known and measureable adjustments that should be made to the budgeted data.  In 
addition, inflation factors were also estimated and applied to the FY 2014 baseline data.  The 
adjustments made are discussed in more detail below. 
Salaries and Benefits 
To project future personnel costs, the Project Team ap plied an inflation factor of 10 % in FY 
2015 and 5% thereafter to all Personnel Services line-items.  These factors were used per the 
City Staff’s recommendations. 
Utilities Expense 
The City is a member of the Texas Coalition of Affordable Power (“TCAP”); therefore, the 
Project Team utilized the TCAP Energy Rate projections plus customer growth to project 
electricity and gas expenses.  The TCAP has projected the rates to remain unchanged through 
FY 2017. As a result, the utilities inflation factor used in the Study is equal to the customer 
growth factor of 6% from FY 2015 through FY 2017.  The City is expecting build -out in FY 
2018, so no customer growth is anticipated beyond FY 2017.  In FY 2018 and FY 2019 the 
utilities are escalated based off a general inflation factor of 2.73%.  This rate represents the 
average annual increase in the Municipal Cost Index (“MCI”) over the last twenty (20) years.1 
Fuel Expense 
The Project Team utilized the Annual Energy Outlook 2014 fuel projections to determine an 
inflation factor for all budgeted line -items for  motor vehicle  fuel2.  In the publication, it is 
projected the fuel rates will remain stagnant and even potentially drop over the next five (5) 
years.  To be conservative, the Project Team held fuel costs steady thereby using an inflation 
rate of 0%. 
                                                            
1 The Municipal Cost Index (“MCI”), published by American City and County Magazine, is similar to the 
Consumer Price Index (“CPI”) in that is tracks the increased cost of a “market basket” of goods.  The 
CPI tracks consumer goods, such as the cost of a haircut, milk, and eggs.  On the other hand, the MCI 
tracks goods applicable to a City, such as cement, construction machinery, office supplies, etc. 
2 The Annual Energy Outlook, published annually by the U. S. Energy Information Administration, 
presents yearly projections and analysis of energy topics including natural gas, motor gasoline, fuel 
oils, electricity, and propane. 
 
Revenue Requirement 
 
City of Murphy Final Report 2-3 
Chemicals Expense 
The twenty (20) year average Producer Price Index (“PPI”) for Water Treating Compounds 
plus customer growth were utilized to calculate an 8.15% inflation rate for chemicals through 
FY 2017.3  In FY 2018 and FY 2019 the inflation factor decreases to 2.15% as a result of no 
customer growth in those years. 
Water Meters 
The purchase of water meters are directly correlated with the number of customers a utility  
serves.  As new customers sign up for service, new meters must be purchased and installed.  
Therefore, the water meter line -item is escalated using the customer growth factor of 6% 
through FY 2 017 and 0% for the remainder of the Study period.  Please note that this input 
into the Study assumes that the City’s existing meters have sufficient life to not require 
replacement prior to FY 2019.  In the event this assumption proves false, additional f unds 
may be needed for future meter replacement.   
Postage / Shipping / Delivery Expense 
An inflation factor of 8.73% has been applied to all postage  and freight line-item expenses.  
This factor represents a 6% increase in customers plus general inflation of 2.73%.  
Lost and Unaccounted for Water Expense 
The NTMWD currently supplies water to the City.  The cost of the water is included as a pass -
through rate to customers and therefore is excluded from the City’s cost of service.  
However, to project the rem aining cost of lost and unaccounted for water the Project Team 
calculated the cost of water loss each year using the NTWMD rate projections and projected 
consumption. 
Inflow & Infiltration Expense 
The NTMWD currently treats the City’s collected wastewater.  Clear estimates of the future 
cost of this treatment were not able to be determined.  Given this, the Project Team 
calculated I & I based off historical billed flow and expenditures. 
Transfer to Other Funds 
The City annually makes a transfer to other Funds.  To be conservative, the Project Team held 
the transfer constant and did not escalate it above the FY 2014 budgeted amount. 
Existing Debt Service 
Debt Service for the utility was projected based on the debt service schedules for utility -
related debt issuance.   
                                                            
3 The Producer Price Index (“PPI”) measures the average change over time in the selling prices 
received by domestic producers for their output.  It is published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor and 
Statistics. 
 
Section 2 
 
2-4 City of Murphy Final Report 
Future Debt Service 
Based on information received from the City’s Capital Improvement Plan, over the Study 
period, the City is in need of approximately $7.6 million in water capital improvements and 
$888,400 in sewer capital improvements (stat ed in current dollars).  Once inflated based on  
an average annual 3.31% increase in construction cost, the total requirements through FY 
2019 are approximately $9.1 million. 4  Currently, the City’s existing debt service extends 
beyond FY 2019.  In order t o assist the City in funding capital improvements but minimizing 
the impact on customers, the Project Team has assumed a debt issuance of $4.6 million in 
water debt and $113,912 in sewer debt in FY 2018 with a 20 year term at a 4.5% interest 
rate.  The anticipated annual payment is $364,298. 
Revenue Offsets 
In order to isolate the revenues that are required from rates to cover expenses associated 
with providing retail service, it is necessary to subtract other utility -related revenues.  The 
revenue offsets identified in this Study correlate with the budgeted values in the FY 2014 
budget.  The Water Meter and Reconnect Fees were escalated based off a 6% customer 
growth factor through FY 2017 and 0% thereafter.  All remaining revenues were escalated 
using a general inflation factor of 2.73%. 
All other Budgeted Line-Items 
Other line -items not specifically discussed above were escalated based on the 2.73% MCI 
inflation rate previously discussed. 
Appendix B attached to this report illustrates the rate revenue requirement of the utility 
projected over the Study timeframe. 
Allocation of Revenue Requirement 
Once the revenue requirement is developed, it is necessary to allocate the revenue to the 
individual water and sewer functions so that the appropriate level of revenue is recovered 
from the respective customer groups .  This is particularly important in order to send  the

ESTIMATED RATES 
In evaluating the performance of existing water and sewer rates and to project future water 
and sewer rates, some estimation of billed water consumption and billed sewer flow is 
required.  In  making this estimation, it is necessary to consider a period of normal 
precipitation.  If data involving abnormal weather patterns is utilized (i.e., unusually low or 
excessive precipitation), then the resulting revenue estimates could be too high or too low.  
For purposes of this Study, the Project Team reviewed consumption data from October 2009  
through March 2014 and utilized the consumption per connection in months when the rainfall 
was closest to normal for a 12 month period.  This projected period, known as the “Test Year” 
was used to reflect normal system operation. 
Water Rates 
Rate Structure 
The City’s water rate structure currently consists of a two -part rate design consisting of a 
minimum monthly charge, which escalates based on the size of a customer’s water meter, 
along with a five -tiered volumetric rate structure wherein a customer pays m ore, per unit of 
consumption, as more water is utilized.   
Standards promulgated by the American Water Works Association (“AWWA”) as well as the 
Texas Water Conservation Implementation Task Force’s Best Management Practices (“TWCITF 
BMP”) guide are used in  evaluating the adequacy of the City’s existing rate design.  The 
TWCITF BMP recommends a 50% increase in rates between rate blocks.  The Project Team 
reviewed the City’s existing rate structure and is of the opinion that the level of consumption 
allowed for in each volumetric rate block is currently adequate;  however, a 15% volumetric 
rate differential between blocks is recommended to meet the City’s goals and objectives.  In 
addition, the Project Team believes the rate differential between meter sizes sh ould be 
adjusted to reflect the AWWA meter equivalency standards based on a ¾ -inch meter.  In 
addition, a reduction in the meter charge is recommended to balance customer affordability 
with revenue demands.   
Projected Rates 
In calculating projected water rates, the Project Team must not only consider the cost of 
service but also take into account the City’s financial policies.  Currently, it is our 
understanding that the City strives to maintain a debt service coverage ratio (“DSC”) of 1.1 
times net revenues.  In other words, gross revenues less operation and maintenance expenses 
should generate sufficient monies to service the City’s water and wastewater debt plus 10%.  
Further, the Days of Cash on Hand policy requires  maintaining 25% of total expenditures  in 
ending Fund Balance .  The City currently has approximately $2.4 million in cash and cash 
equivalents but falls $757,716 short of meeting the Days Cash on Hand financial requirement  
of $2 million in FY 2015 .  In the Project Team’s opinion, it is critica lly important that the City

Sewer Rates 
Rate Structure 
The City’s current sewer rate is similar to its water rate.  Each customer pays a minimum 
service charge, which does not include any flow, and a volumetric charge per 1,000 gallons of 
sewer flow contributed to the system.  For residential customers, billed sewer flow is based 
on the customer’s water consumption during the winter months of November, January, and 
February.  On the other hand, commercial customers are billed sewer flow based on actual 
water consumption.   
It is the opinion of the Project Team that the City’s existing rate structure should be modified 
so as to charge all customers the same volumetric rate under the assumpti on that all 
customers produce sewage of the same domestic strength.  Further, the Project Team 
recommends setting one standard minimum charge for all rate classes and reducing the 
current rate which will improve the impact on lower volume and lower income customers.  
However, doing so destabilizes the revenue stream which means the City must recover more 
revenue through the volumetric rates.  As a result, the Project Team recommends increasing 
the volumetric charge significantly to reflect the cost of waste water treatment from NTMWD 
and to ensure the financial integrity of the wastewater service.

As with water, the sewer rates must not only generate enough revenue to recover the cost of 
service, but the DSC ratio and the Days Cash on Hand met rics must be met as well.  As 
discussed previously and shown in Table 3 -2, the combined water and sewer revenue  under 
current rates does not satisfy the financial policy requirements of the City.  In addition, the 
sewer rate revenues generated from existin g sewer rates do not recover the sewer cost of 
service.

RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
1. In order to assist in maintaining the financial stability of the City’s Water and Sewer 
Fund, sufficient rates should be put in place to ensure full cost recovery through user 
rate revenue.  Further, we recommend that the City continuously monitor the 
financial performance of the Water and Sewer Fund and adjust rates as necessary to 
maintain the financial stability of the water and sewer utility. 
 
2. It is recommended that t he City implement a rate adjustment for the water and 
sewer systems effective October 1, 2014 in order to maintain the financial stability of 
the utility.   
 
3. Assuming no reduction in General Fund expenditures, the reduction in the General 
Fund Transfer would require funding from another revenue source such as property 
taxes.  In order to refrain from raising taxes to cover the General Fund expenses, we 
recommend maintaining the historical transfer amount. 
 
4. While sufficient unrestricted cash and cash equivalents are currently available to 
serve as an operating reserve of the utility, the level of available funds should be 
monitored and adjusted as necessary to ensure the utility maintains sufficient 
reserve levels. 
 
5. The Project Team recommends the City consider adjusting the ex isting rate blocks so 
that the first rate block include s the residential winter average of 7,000 gallons and 
the second rate block include the residential annual average of 13,200 gallons.  Doing 
so ensures the majority of customers are being billed in the first volumetric block. 
 
6. It is our understanding that t he City has considered itemizing the customer bills to 
include a City charge and a NTMWD charge.  However, w e recommend presenting 
one combined rate on the customer bills  to facilitate administration of the rate 
structure.  In order to facilitate the transparency goals of the city, publishing the 
separate charges on the City’s website will provide sufficient detail for  customers

Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae Zipcar Robin Chase is the Founder and CEO of Zipcar, the largest car sharing company in the world. Robin is an Alumna of Springboard’s New England Innovation cohort in 2000. Robin co-founded Zipcar in 2000 and co-wrote its first business plan after hearing about a car-sharing venture in Europe. Zipcar disrupted the transportation industry by allowing customers to book cars on demand by the hour or day. Zipcar went public in 2011 and was later acquired by Avis Budget Group in 2013. We are proud of Robin’s continued dedication to transportation innovation and her thought leadership across transportation, entrepreneurship, and technology innovation. Robin Chase Founder & CEO Zipcar Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae Constant Contact Gail Goodman is the former Chairman, President, and CEO of Constant Contact (NASDAQ: CTCT), and is a prestigious Alumna from Springboard’s 2000 New England Innovation cohort. Gail startedConstant Contact (then Roving Software) which enables users to engage email marketing campaigns and nurture customer relationships. In her 16-year tenure as CEO, Gail led the company to a successful IPO in 2007. She left the company shortly after its acquisition by Endurance in 2016 for $1.1 billion. She continues to be an innovator and we are proud of Gail’s continued commitment to making a better world through inclusive entrepreneurship. Gail Goodman Chairman, President & CEO Constant Contact Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae The RealReal E-Commerce pioneer, Julie Wainwright is the founder and CEO of The RealReal (NASDAQ: REAL). Julie is an Alumna of Springboard’s All Things Media 2008 Innovation Cohort and the recepient of Springboard’s 2016 Northstar Award. The Real Real is an online marketplace for authenticated, consigned luxury goods. The company uses a rigorous authentication process to provide a safe and reliable platform for consumers to buy and sell their luxury items. As a sustainable company, The RealReal gives new life to pieces by brands such as Gucci to Cartier by providing accessible consignment to shoppers 60 countries across the globe. The RealReal went public in 2019 with a $2.3 billion valuation. We are proud of the work Julie is doing to disrupt the fashion industry through the continued innovation at The RealReal. Julie Wainwright Founder & CEO The RealReal Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae Aura Biosciences Aura Biosciences (NASDAQ: AURA) founder Elisabet de los Pinos, PhD is an Alumna of Springboard’s Life Sciences Innovation 2012 cohort. Her vision to develop a VDC technology platform to treat cancer tumors has positioned Aura as a market leader in the urologic and ocular oncology space. Aura is working to establish a new standard of care through a new class of oncology targeted therapies that deliver meaningful therapeutic benefits to a range of cancer indications with high unmet need. They are driven by a passion and commitment to science and especially the patients battling cancer who are relying on these new therapies. Aura went public in 2021. We are proud of our Springboard Alumna Elisabet de los Pinos and her courageous and innovative work. Elisabet de los Pinos Founder & CEO Aura Biosciences Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae Marrone Bio Innovations ArgaQuest founder and CEO, Pamela Marrone is an Alumna of Springboard’s Silicon Valley 2004 Innovation cohort. She founded ArgaQuest in 1995 with the purpose to develop environementally friendly products for pest management. heir green products control a broad spectrum of pests and diseases and offer farmers integrated pest management programs to minimize development of resistance and maximize crop yields. In Pamela’s 11-year tenure as CEO, she raised over $60 million in venture capital. AgraQuest was sold to Bayer for $425 million plus $75 million in milestone payments in 2012. We at Springboard champion Pamela’s continued innovation in the food & agriculture industry. Pamela Marrone Founder and CEO Marrone Bio Innovations Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae Ondine Biomedical Carolyn Cross is the Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Ondine Biomedical Inc. (LON: OBI), a Vancouver-based medical devices company. Carolyn is an Alumna of Springboard’s Life Science innovation cohort where she presented Odine in 2017. Ondine is a life sciences company that focuses on the development of photodisinfection-based therapies to provide solutions to drug-resistant infections. They are focused on developing and commercializing novel antimicrobial therapies that address significant patient needs, are environmentally safe, provide substantial public health benefits, are easy to deploy, and cost a fraction of the infections they target. Ondine made its debut on the London Stock Exchange in December 2021. Springboard is proud to call Carolyn an Alumna for her continued work in women’s empowerment and innovation. Carolyn Cross Chairman & CEO Ondine Biomedical Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae EverlyWell Julia Cheek is the Founder and CEO of EverlyWell and an Alumna of Springboard’s Tech Innovation Hub 2016 cohort. EverlyWell is a digital health company poised to disrupt the 25 billion dollar lab testing industry by providing consumers with at-home lab tests that include insightful, easy-to-understand results. EverlyWell was founded in 2015 to provide consumers access to at-home lab tests that include insightful, easy-to-understand results. As of 2021, Everlywell had raised $325 million in funding, and has a post-money valuation in the range of $1 billion to $10 billion. Julia continues to break barriers and we are proud to call her a Sprinboard Alumna. Julia Cheek Co-Founder & CEO EverlyWell Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae Medable Dr. Michelle Longmire is the Co-Founder and CEO of Medable and is a notable Alumna from Springboard’s Digital Health 2017 innovation cohort. She co-founded Medable with a vision to open research to the world through a decentralized clinical trial platform proven to help get effective therapies to patients faster. Medable uses a cloud-based approach to making participation in clinical trials more consumer-friendly and more equitable. The company is privately held and based in Palo Alto, California. Medable has raised $521 million in funding with a $2.1 billion valuation. Dr. Longmire’s passion for medicine and the human experience makes Springboard proud to call her an Alumna. Michelle Longmire Co-Founder & CEO Medable Spotlighting Alumnae Success Stories Across Industries Alumnae 51job Kathleen Chien is an Alumna of Springboard’s Silicon Valley 2000 innovation cohort. In September 2004, 51job successfully completed its IPO on NASDAQ and in 2022 51job became a privately held company after completing a merger with Garnet Faith Limited. Kathleen is a pioneer and we are proud to call her an Alumna of Springboard. AskBio’s therapeutic focus on neuromuscular, central nervous system, cardiovascular and metabolic diseases now has clinical trials underway for Pompe disease, Parkinson’s disease, and congestive heart failure. AskBio became a wholly-owned, independently operated, subsidiary of Bayer AG in late 2020 as a cornerstone of its newly formed Cell & Gene Therapy (CGT) platform.
